When the two data sets are aggregated, the VMT proportion still favors urban other roads over urban freeways. For combination-unit short-haul trucks traveling in the combined FleetDNA and CE-CERT data set, they spend 59% of their time on urban other roads out of the total time they drive on urban roads. Because they only spent less than 3% on rural roads, this proportion is very similar to the 57.8% they spend on urban other roads out of all road types, but we recommend updating MOVES based solely on the fraction spent between the two urban road types for sources other than combination-unit long-haul. In MOVES currently, the combination-unit short-haul truck proportion on urban freeways out of all roads is 24.4% and 25.5% on urban other roads, which totals 50%. We recommend keeping this overall percentage at 50 but adjusting the time spent on urban other roads to 29.5% of all roads (i.e., 59% times 50%) and urban freeways to 20.5% of the total (41% times 50%). Similarly, for single-unit short-haul trucks, we recommend updating the urban percentages to 36.1% on urban other roads—a slight increase over the current 34%—and 21.5% on urban freeways to match the 62.7% that FleetDNA and CE-CERT trucks combined drive on urban other roads compared to all urban roads. Refuse trucks spent significantly more time on urban other roads compared to urban freeways; in the combined data set, they spent 82.7% of urban road driving on urban other roads. MOVES accordingly, we would recommend 48.3% of total time on urban other roads and 10.1% on urban freeways. This adjustment maintains the MOVES default of 58.5% on urban roads to not bias the national defaults based on collecting data from urban refuse fleets. For transit, the ratio of urban other road driving to urban freeway driving is roughly equal to current MOVES defaults. MOVES gives 38.6% of driving to urban other roads out of all roads, and to match the combined FleetDNA and CE-CERT data, this proportion would only be changed to 38.1% and urban freeways to 26.4%. School bus distributions may be shifted slightly in favor of other roads, but we would not recommend eliminating miles spent on road type 4 as the graph may imply, because FleetDNA only contained data from four school buses. We also would not recommend using the other bus source type distributions directly because they are also based on a small sample of buses.
